needs/ask: You built curl, and it runs. Copy just its folder to another machine, and it may not start at all.
needs/lean: A program leans on other things: shared libraries, certificates, a shell. Most systems hope those are already there.
needs/refs: Nix does not hope. For every store path, it records which other store paths that one points at. Those are its references.
needs/list: Here is curl, with a few of its references: OpenSSL, zlib and lib S S H two.
scan/who: Nobody writes that list by hand. Nix finds it.
scan/hash: Every input of a build has a hash in its store path, and hashes that long do not turn up by accident.
scan/scan: So after a build, Nix reads the output, byte by byte, looking for the hash of each input.
scan/hit: The hash of OpenSSL is inside the curl binary, so curl references OpenSSL.
scan/miss: The compiler was an input too, but its hash is nowhere in the result. It was needed to build curl, not to run it, so it is not a reference.
closure/more: References have references of their own. OpenSSL points at the C library, and so does zlib.
closure/walk: Start at one path and follow every arrow, until there is nowhere new to go. Every path you touched, the start included, is its closure.
closure/once: A path counts once, however many arrows reach it. The C library is one folder, shared by all of them.
closure/count: For this small curl, that is five store paths.
copy/whole: A closure is complete: nothing inside it points outside it.
copy/unit: That makes it the thing you copy. Nix copy sends a path and everything in its closure.
copy/skip: If the server already has a path, Nix skips it: the name says it is the same one. Here the C library stays put, and four paths go across.
copy/run: Every reference still points at the same place under slash nix slash store, so curl runs there exactly as it ran here.
